extracted.intended_audience: students of law, gentlemen, members of the legal profession, and university audience
extracted.subtask_description: Expository legal treatise (Blackstone's Commentaries) setting out who should study the law, why, and what knowledge and professional qualities are required of judges, magistrates, jurors, legislators, clergy, and legal practitioners. Also includes editorial/transcription and Project Gutenberg redistribution requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the laws of one's own country
rubrics_metrics.description: A competent knowlege of the laws of that society, in which we live, is the proper accomplishment of every gentleman and scholar; an highly useful, I had almost said essential, part of liberal and polite education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone argues the utility of legal knowledge for all ranks: to protect natural rights, to conform to equitable rules of action, and to avoid living in society 'without knowing the obligations which it lays him under.' Examples given include property management, jury service, magistracy, parliamentary service, and general civic duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic understanding of estates and conveyancing for landed gentlemen
rubrics_metrics.description: The thorough comprehension of estates and conveyancing is perhaps too laborious for any but a lawyer by profession; yet the understanding of a few leading principles, relating to estates and conveyancing, may form some check and guard upon a gentleman's inferior agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical expectation: gentlemen of independent estates should learn leading principles to avoid gross imposition by agents and to manage settlements, entails, descents, and incumbrances prudently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of formal requirements for wills and testaments
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy of all laws has made some forms necessary in the wording of last wills and testaments, and more with regard to their attestation. An ignorance in these must always be of dangerous consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated consequence: omission of one or two formal words or insufficient witnesses can frustrate a testator's intent and vest the estate contrary to intention. Practical criterion: ensure requisite formal words and witness numbers when executing wills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence of jurors where law and fact are blended
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentlemen called upon to serve upon juries are frequently to decide, and that upon their oaths, questions of nice importance, in the solution of which some legal skill is requisite; especially where the law and the fact, as it often happens, are intimately blended together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone notes poor juror capacity 'debased their authority' and causes greater judicial intervention; thus jurors should have sufficient legal understanding to render proper verdicts when legal interpretation is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrates must understand their authority and the law
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to attain desirable ends, it is necessary that the magistrate should understand his business; and have not only the will, but the power also, (under which must be included the knowlege) of administring legal and effectual justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If magistrates mistake their authority through passion or ignorance they become objects of contempt and censure; criterion: magistrates should be legally informed to maintain order, punish offenders, protect industrious people, and heal petty differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members of Parliament should be instructed in existing law and constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are ambitious of receiving so high a trust, would also do well to remember its nature and importance... They are the guardians of the English constitution; the makers, repealers, and interpreters of the English laws...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone insists that legislators ought to know the old law before voting for new laws; 'how unbecoming must it appear in a member of the legislature to vote for a new law, who is utterly ignorant of the old!' — criterion: legislators require thorough constitutional and statutory knowledge to legislate responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute drafting ought to be done by those versed in the common law
rubrics_metrics.description: If acts of parliament were after the old fashion penned by such only as perfectly knew what the common law was before the making of any act of parliament concerning that matter... then should very few questions in law arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone (via Coke) critiques 'ill-judging and unlearned legislators' and attributes statutory confusion to drafting by those who do not understand common law; criterion: drafters should be informed in common law and prior statutes to avoid ambiguity, provisoes, and later constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peers and nobility must be legally informed for their judicial and senatorial roles
rubrics_metrics.description: They are not only... hereditary counsellors of the crown, and judges upon their honour of the lives of their brother-peers, but also arbiters of the property of all their fellow-subjects, and that in the last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because their decisions are final and binding on inferior courts, peers must be masters of points they are to decide; criterion: the nobility should possess substantial legal knowledge given their irrevocable judicial responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial competence required at all levels, especially superior judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Should a judge in the most subordinate jurisdiction be deficient in the knowlege of the law, it would reflect infinite contempt upon himself... But how much more serious... is the case of a superior judge, if without any skill in the laws he will boldly venture to decide a question... where, if he chances to judge wrong, he does an injury of the most alarming nature, an injury without possibility of redress!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: superior judges must have deep legal knowledge because their judgments have finality and may do irreparable harm if erroneous; inferior judges' errors can be corrected, but superior judges bear higher responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy should know laws peculiar to ecclesiastical functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The clergy... have also abundant reason, considered merely as clergymen, to be acquainted with many branches of the law, which are almost peculiar and appropriated to themselves alone. Such are the laws relating to advowsons, institutions, and inductions; to simony... to tithes... to marriages...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion: clergy must understand church-law topics (advowsons, simony, uniformity, residence, pluralities, tithes, marriages) because statutes consign these subjects to their order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicians (and others) may benefit from limited legal knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: For the gentlemen of the faculty of physic, I must frankly own that I see no special reason, why they in particular should apply themselves to the study of the law; unless in common with other gentlemen... it might frequently be of use to families upon sudden emergencies, if the physician were acquainted with the doctrine of last wills and testaments...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: while not essential, professionals like physicians should have limited procedural legal knowledge (e.g., formal execution of wills) for practical emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil and canon lawyers must know how Roman/canon law interacts with English law
rubrics_metrics.description: It becomes highly necessary for every civilian and canonist that would act with safety as a judge, or with prudence and reputation as an advocate, to know in what cases and how far the English laws have given sanction to the Roman; in what points the latter are rejected...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: those practising in spiritual/maritime courts must discern where foreign laws are received, where they are supplemental to common law (king's maritime, military, ecclesiastical law), and where they are controlled or prohibited by the common law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of teaching municipal (common) law in universities
rubrics_metrics.description: A competent knowlege of the laws of that society, in which we live, is the proper accomplishment of every gentleman and scholar... The university of Oxford appoints that one of the three questions... shall relate to the common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and institutional criterion: universities should include common law in curricula so that jurists, civil servants, and gentlemen are not ignorant of municipal law; the university statutes are cited to justify formal instruction in common law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/transcription principles for reproducing historical texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir William Blackstone's Commentaries... contains a number of archaic spellings... that have been preserved as they appear in the original. All such spellings have been verified using the Oxford English Dictionary. Inconsistencies in spelling, punctuation, hyphenation, capitalization, and italicization have also been preserved. Obvious printer errors have been preserved and marked with a [Transcriber's Note]. Long s in the original has been modernized as modern s. The archaic convention of placing quotation marks at the beginning of each line of a quotation has also been modernized to quotation marks only at the beginning and end of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcription standard: preserve original archaic spellings (verified), preserve inconsistencies, mark printer errors, modernize long s and line-beginning quotation marks; this balances fidelity to the original with readability and explicit error-marking.
